info.bio:
Joy Division fue una banda post-punk inglesa, formada en 1976 en Salford, en el área metropolitana de Manchester, Reino Unido. Se disolvió en mayo de 1980 tras el suicidio de su cantante, Ian Curtis. El resto de miembros del grupo crearon un grupo nuevo, New Order, meses después.

Aunque tuvieron un éxito modesto en su carrera, y lanzaron sólo dos álbumes de estudio, Joy Division ha sido aclamado desde entonces como uno de los más innovadores, evocativos e influyentes grupos de su tiempo. Tras la muerte del cantante y líder del grupo, Ian Curtis, la banda pasó a ser  leyenda , convirtiéndose Curtis en uno de los músicos más influyentes de todos los tiempos.

Joy Division fue etiquetado por mucha gente como una banda oscura y depresiva, debido a lo inhóspito de su música y al suicidio de Ian Curtis. Sin embargo, los restantes miembros de la banda y la gente que conocieron lo han negado siempre.

Sus influencias van desde el proto-punk: The Velvet Underground, The Stooges; el punk: The Sex Pistols; e incluso el glam: David Bowie. Todas estas bandas bordeando más siempre un ámbito alternativo. Se podría decir que Joy Division tomó de estas bandas un poco y lo mezcló en un estilo que sólo pocos han podido interpretar: el post-punk. Del proto-punk tomó su excentricidad y lírica, del punk tomó la fuerza escénica y musical y, finalmente, tomó del glam su estética.

Suicidarse a los 23 años, no parece un acto de una persona cuerda, pero dejar pistas que den significado a su fatal determinación de ahorcarse en su casa, denota un asunto denso y lleno de lucidez. Ian Curtis, cantante y líder de la legendaria banda inglesa, se ahorcó en la cocina de su casa el 18 de mayo de 1980, su nota suicida sólo decía sobriamente: “En este momento quisiera estar muerto. No aguanto más”. Otras teorias, hablan de que su suicidio se debio a que quiso cumplir con el mito de la estrella del rock´n´roll que muere joven dejando un bonito cadáver.

Su esposa Deborah encontró el cuerpo colgando de una soga, una botella de whisky vacía, las fotos de su boda y la de su hija en el sofá, el disco ‘The idiot’ de Iggy Pop tocando interminablemente y señalada en una revista Tv guía, la película Stroszek (1977) de Werner Herzog.

Su mente atormentada por un desencanto por la vida, amargo pesimismo, su alma muerta, sus constantes ataques de epilepsia, lo llevaban a refugiarse en la lectura de los Existencialistas, donde encontró las respuestas: el ser humano está abandonado a su suerte, solo contamos con nosotros mismos, existimos para estar solos, allá arriba en el cielo, solo hay un enorme vacío. 

Como anécdota decir que la canción "She Lost Control" la escribió Curtis inspirándose en un ataque de epilepsia que le dio a una chica mientras era atendida por éste en su lugar de trabajo, días más tarde este se puso en contacto con su familia y se enteró de que había fallecido. Este hecho lo afectó mucho y en ello encontró la inspiración.

En la escena final de la película del director alemán Herzog, una gallina hipnotizada gira y gira alrededor de un árbol. Al final de su álbum The Idiot (1977), Iggy Pop canta “Aunque trato de matarme/ vuelves a ponerme de nuevo en línea”. Esas son las pistas que dejó, además de las letras de las canciones de su grupo Joy Division. 

Años después, el legado de Ian Curtis deja huella en una generación de jóvenes desencantados, desanimados por un futuro incierto, influenciando a grupos como The Cure y U2, y más recientemente a Interpol, con sus riffs hipnóticos, y Trent Reznor a veces se siente el hijo obrero de Ian Curtis. Cabe destacar también otro grupos que se vieron fuertemente influenciados, tales como The Killers, que debe su nombre a la letra de una canción de Joy Division y Radiohead el cual homenajearon la canción Ceremony en una apasionante versión.

El grupo dejó alrededor de 50 canciones grabadas y publicó tan sólo dos discos de estudio. El primero de ellos se tituló ‘Unknown Pleasures’ y se editó en 1979 en el sello Factory Records, propiedad del periodista Tony Wilson. El siguiente, "Closer", salió tras la muerte de Curtis y está considerado como una de las joyas de la historia del rock. Curtis, que sufría epilepsia, patentó un personalísimo estilo de baile con movimientos espasmódicos que estaban ‘inspirados’ en sus ataques reales. En alguna ocasión los miembros del grupo no estaban realmente seguros si Curtis estaba bailando o sufriendo un ataque, ya que las luces de los escenarios agravaban su enfermedad.

Joy Division debe su nombre a las muchachas que entretenían a los soldados nazis en los campos de concentración judíos, aunque pareciera erróneamente que el verdadero significado es "Separados de la felicidad" . Adoptaron este nombre tras el inicial, que fue "Warsaw", tras ser demandados por Warsaw Pakt y darles la razón los tribunales a éstos últimos. 

Curtis fue incinerado y sus cenizas enterradas en Macclesfield, con la inscripción "Love Will Tear Us Apart" en su lápida. Este epitafio, escogido por Deborah Curtis, es el título de la canción más conocida de Joy Division. "Closer", el segundo álbum de Joy Division se lanzó de forma póstuma en 1980, 2 meses después del suicidio de Curtis.

info.wikipedia:
Joy Division fue una banda de post-punk inglesa, formada en 1976 en Salford, Gran Mánchester. Originalmente llamada Stiff Kittens, la banda estuvo formada por Ian Curtis, Bernard Sumner,[n. 1]​ Peter Hook y Stephen Morris.

Joy Division evolucionó de sus influencias punk rock iniciales (de acuerdo con el crítico musical Jon Savage, "no era punk, pero estaba directamente inspirada por su energía")[1]​ para posteriormente desarrollar un sonido y un estilo del cual fue pionero, llamado post-punk, junto con bandas como Siouxsie And The Banshees y The Cure, pues no solo poseían un sonido siniestro, sino que sus letras estaban obsesionadas con la desesperación y la muerte, productos de la epilepsia que padecía Curtis.

Su EP debut, An Ideal for Living, atrajo la atención de Tony Wilson, una personalidad de la televisión de Mánchester. El álbum debut de Joy Division, Unknown Pleasures, fue lanzado en el sello discográfico de Wilson, Factory Records, y provocó la aclamación de la crítica británica. Curtis se vio afectado por la depresión y por problemas personales, incluyendo la disolución de su matrimonio y sus agudas crisis de epilepsia. El cantautor encontraba cada vez más difícil presentarse en vivo y a menudo tenía convulsiones durante sus espectáculos.

En mayo de 1980, en la víspera de la primera gira de la banda por los Estados Unidos y abrumado por problemas, Curtis se suicidó ahorcándose, a los veintitrés años. Joy Division lanzó póstumamente su segundo álbum, titulado Closer (1980), y el sencillo «Love Will Tear Us Apart» se convirtió en su lanzamiento más exitoso en los rankings. Después de la muerte de Curtis, los miembros restantes de la banda formaron New Order.

Inspirados por la presentación de los Sex Pistols en el Manchester Lesser Free Trade Hall, el 20 de julio de 1976, Bernard Sumner y Peter Hook formaron un grupo junto a su amigo Terry Mason. Sumner compró una guitarra, Hook compró un bajo y Mason una batería. El grupo colocó un anuncio en una tienda de discos de Mánchester, reclutando así a Ian Curtis como cantante. Curtis conocía a Sumner, Hook y Mason de presentaciones previas, ya que también estuvo esa noche en el público del concierto de los Sex Pistols junto a su esposa, Deborah. Richard Boon y Pete Shelley, respectivos mánager y guitarrista del grupo punk Buzzcocks, sugirieron el nombre Stiff Kittens para el grupo. Aunque el nombre Stiff Kittens apareció en algunos panfletos de presentaciones, al grupo nunca le agradó ni lo aceptó oficialmente.

Debido a que carecía de confianza en sus capacidades como batería, Mason abandonó el grupo el día anterior a la primera presentación en el Electric Circus para transformarse en el representante del grupo. Para la ocasión, fue reemplazado por Tony Tabac. Momentos antes de aquella presentación junto a Buzzcocks y a Penetration el 29 de mayo de 1977, el grupo cambió su nombre a Warsaw, en homenaje a la canción de David Bowie y Brian Eno, llamada «Warszawa». Cinco semanas después, tras seis presentaciones, Tabac fue reemplazado por el baterista del grupo punk The Panik, Steve Brotherdale. Grabaron Warsaw Demo el 18 de julio de 1977, cinta que contenía cinco crudas canciones de punk.

Después del demo, Brotherdale fue despedido de una manera extraña: mientras todo el grupo iba en una camioneta, le pidieron que bajara a revisar los neumáticos de las llantas porque se sentían bajas. Al bajar a revisar, el coche aceleró y se fue sin él. Stephen Morris fue contratado como reemplazante de Brotherdale tras ver un anuncio en la ventana de una tienda de música. Fue contratado en primera instancia puesto que Curtis recordaba haber asistido al mismo colegio que Morris. Curtis era dos años mayor que Morris. En comparación con los baterías anteriores, Morris encajó bien con los tres miembros restantes.

La música y el género musical del grupo se empezó a definir por este periodo. Las sesiones grabadas en diciembre de 1977 comenzaron a sonar de manera muy distinta al sonido producido en Warsaw Demo.

A comienzos de 1978, para evitar la confusión con el grupo de punk de Londres llamado Warsaw Pakt, Warsaw cambió su nombre a Joy Division. Este nombre, que contrasta con su verdadera traducción de «División Alegría», hace referencia al grupo de mujeres judías usadas como esclavas sexuales en los campos de concentración nazi, representadas en la novela La casa de las muñecas (1955) de Ka-Tzetnik 135633. Aunque la elección del nombre fue de una manera más reflexiva que una forma de luchar contra los tabúes, esta elección, junto con la adopción por parte de Sumner del apellido Albrecht, acumularon en el grupo una serie de críticas de perceptible insensibilidad. Incluso fueron perseguidos por acusaciones de neonazismo, algo que negaron con vigor.[2]​

El primer show de Joy Division fue en el Pip's, Mánchester, el 24 de enero de 1978. El tres y cuatro de mayo de ese año, grabaron para el sello RCA el material de su primer disco. Sin embargo, el productor John Anderson, creyendo que el punk no duraría mucho y sin el consentimiento de los músicos, llenó la grabación de sintetizadores en la mezcla final. La banda estuvo completamente en desacuerdo con esto y el disco nunca fue editado —aunque se convertiría en uno de los bootlegs más conocidos del grupo—. Poco después, Rob Gretton reemplazó a Terry Mason como manager.

Tony Wilson fundó el sello discográfico Factory Records, discográfica con la que el 18 de mayo de ese mismo año firmó contrato con Joy Division. Wilson rellenó dicho contrato con su propia sangre.[cita requerida]

El 9 de junio, Joy Division tocó junto con otras bandas en la apertura del club The Factory de Tony Wilson. El artista Peter Saville diseñó el póster del evento conocido como FAC 1!!. El 27 de diciembre, hicieron su primera actuación en Londres en el Hope And Anchor de Islington frente a alrededor de 30 personas. Este fue, además, el primer concierto por el que cobraron entrada.[cita requerida]

El 14 de febrero de 1979 Joy Division tocó en la BBC, donde grabaron varios temas para el conocido programa de John Peel. Posteriormente sería conocido (y editado) como The 1st Peel Session. Esto les dio bastante publicidad, y en marzo de ese mismo año tocaron como teloneros de The Cure en el Marquee de Londres. En abril de 1979 graban Unknown Pleasures (Placeres Desconocidos en español), la producción fue de Martin Hannett y el diseño de la portada lo realizó Peter Saville. Ambos continuarían trabajando con Joy Division y, posteriormente, con New Order. El disco tuvo muy buenas críticas y vendió bien. A pesar del éxito y las ofertas de sellos grandes, Joy Division decidió quedarse en Factory para poder tener control sobre su música. En noviembre de 1979, la Warner Bros. americana les ofreció un millón de dólares para distribuir su disco en Estados Unidos y hacer algunos vídeos. Nunca respondieron a esta iniciativa y su actitud sería similar cuando, en mayo de 1980, se repitió la oferta en términos más favorables para la banda.

El 31 de agosto de 1979, reunieron a 1200 personas en el Electric Ballroom, Londres, la mayor audiencia que tuvo la banda. El 15 de septiembre aparecieron en la televisión en el programa Something Else, de la BBC —antes habían aparecido un par de veces en Granada TV—. Los violentos movimientos del cantante durante «Transmission» y «She's Lost Control» impresionaron a la audiencia. Pronto llamarían la atención por otras razones. Curtis sufría de epilepsia y con frecuencia tenía convulsiones, espasmos y hasta pérdida del conocimiento. El 26 de noviembre, grabaron por segunda vez con John Peel —The 2nd Peel Session—. Una de las canciones era «Love Will Tear Us Apart» que pronto se convirtió en un clásico de la banda y una de las más conocidas canciones "no grabadas" de Inglaterra: hasta el 10 de abril de 1980, en que fue editada como sencillo, solo era posible oírla en los conciertos.

En diciembre de ese mismo año, iniciaron una breve gira por Europa que se prolongó hasta enero y durante el cual terminó el affaire de Ian con Annik Honore, una fanática de origen belga, que había empezado un par de meses antes. De esta gira es famoso el concierto en el club Paradiso de Ámsterdam. No solo porque en el tocaron dos sets consecutivos con un total de 17 canciones, sino también por ser otro de los discos piratas más famosos de la banda. En marzo de 1980, la revista Sordide Sentimental editó un disco de siete pulgadas llamado Licht Und Blindheit, del que se editaron 1.578 discos numerados sin silencios entre las canciones. Fue una producción de Martin Hannett que incluía las canciones «Dead Souls» y «Atmosphere», que Joy Division había grabado en octubre del año anterior.

En marzo de 1980, grabaron el material de su segundo disco, Closer y el sencillo «Love Will Tear Us Apart». El tratamiento médico de Curtis no ayudaba y su condición general parecía agravarse a medida que la agenda de la banda aumentaba. Sus ataques continuaban, incluso en escena. Durante un concierto como teloneros de los The Stranglers, perdió el control de sí mismo y derribó la batería. Tres días después intentó suicidarse con una sobredosis de fenobarbital. La noche siguiente debió ser reemplazado en el concierto del Derby Hall por Bury. La gente, que esperaba a Curtis, comenzó un verdadero caos donde no faltaron golpes y botellas volando. Curtis vio todo entre bastidores y no pudo dejar de sentirse responsable.

El 2 de mayo, Joy Division dio su último concierto en Birmingham. Este concierto, la única vez que tocaron «Ceremony», aparecería luego en el disco doble Still. Dos semanas después, iban a partir a Estados Unidos para hacer su primera gira en ese país.

En la mañana del domingo 18 de mayo de 1980, Curtis estaba viendo el filme Stroszek, al terminar el filme puso el disco The Idiot de Iggy Pop y tras escribir una nota a su esposa, se ahorcó en la cocina de su casa, con una cuerda de tender la ropa. Dos meses después, «Love Will Tear Us Apart» alcanzó el Top 20 de los charts británicos, mientras que Closer llegó al Top 10. Cuando parecía que eso era todo y que la carrera de la banda estaba terminada, Sumner, Hook y Morris formaron New Order. El grupo continuaría el camino de Joy Division incorporando otros ritmos y ampliando su horizonte de experimentación, pero manteniendo siempre su independencia y calidad. No puede negarse la influencia de Curtis en este cambio de dirección.

Joy Division han referenciado varias formaciones alemanes como Kraftwerk, Can y Neu!.[3]​ Ian Curtis y su banda tenían la costumbre de esperar a su público antes de cada concierto pasando la totalidad de Trans-Europe Express, de Kraftwerk: Stephen Morris, "El matrimonio hombre-máquina durante el funcionamiento [como por Kraftwerk] es algo fantástico".[3]​ El periodo Berlín de David Bowie con el álbum Low tuvo un impacto en el grupo.[4]​ Junto con esto, el rock oscuro de los años 60, con Velvet Underground y The Doors, también inspiró a los músicos de Mánchester. La voz de barítono Curtis ha sido a menudo comparado con el timbre de Jim Morrison. Peter Hook dijo: Siouxsie And The Banshees también eran "una de nuestras mayores influencias [...] de la forma inusual de tocar la guitarra y la batería".[5]​ Stephen Morris también los citó para el ritmo dirigido por el bajo, "la forma en que el primer baterista Kenny Morris tocaba principalmente toms. [...] Los Banshees tenían ese sonido premonitorio, dibujando el futuro desde la oscuridad del pasado. [...] escuchar las sesiones que habían hecho en el programa de John Peel y leer reseñas de conciertos ", sobre ellos lo inspiró.[6]​

A Joy Division les tomó tiempo desarrollar su propio sonido. Como Warsaw, la banda practicaba una "forma inclasificable de hard rock con toques punk". El crítico Simon Reynolds aseguraba que "la originalidad de Joy Division se ponía de manifiesto cuando las canciones se volvían más lentas". La música del grupo adoptó un tono "desparramado"; según Reynolds "el bajo de Peter Hook llevaba la melodía, la guitarra de Bernard Sumner rellenaba los huecos del sonido a base de densos riffs y la batería de Stephen Morris parecía rodear el borde de un cráter". Con el tiempo, Ian Curtis empezó a cantar con voz suave de barítono, a menudo comparable a la de Jim Morrison de The Doors, una de las bandas preferidas de Curtis.

Sumner ejercía como jefe musical no oficial de la banda, como después en New Order. Mientras que Sumner era el guitarrista principal, Curtis solo tocó la guitarra en unas pocas grabaciones y conciertos. En 1979, adquirió una guitarra de la serie Vox Phantom VI Special que, irónicamente, Curtis odiaba tocar, pero los otros insistían en que lo hiciera. Sumner dijo: "tocaba de una forma estrambótica, pero era lo que nos gustaba, porque nadie más que Ian tocaba de aquella manera". Aunque Sumner usaba una guitarra modelo Shergold Custom Masquerader, durante la grabación de Closer empezó a utilizar sintetizadores hechos por él mismo, y Hook usaba bajos Rickenbacker 4001JG, Yamaha BB1200 o Shergold Marathon entre otros modelos y amplificadores Hiwatt para reforzar la melodía.

El productor Martin Hannett se "dedicó a capturar e intensificar el halo tétrico de Joy Division". Hannett creía que el punk rock era sonoramente conservador por su rechazo a utilizar tecnologías de estudio para crear espacio sonoro. El productor se propuso crear un sonido más desarrollado para los discos del grupo. Hannett dijo: "(Joy Division) Eran un regalo para un productor, porque no seguían directrices, ni argumentos".[7]​ Hannett separó y limpió desde su mesa los sonidos de los diferentes instrumentos, incluso las distintas partes de la batería de Morris.

A pesar de su corta carrera y su estatus de "grupo de culto", Joy Division han ejercido una influencia de largo alcance. John Bush, de Allmusic, dice que Joy Division "se convirtieron en la primera banda del movimiento post-punk en enfatizar no la cólera y la energía, sino el estado de ánimo y la palabra, dando pie al advenimiento de la melancólica música alternativa de los 80".

El oscuro y tenebroso sonido del grupo, que Martin Hannett describió en 1979 como "música de baile con sobretonos góticos", presagiaba el nombre del género rock gótico. Mientras en la música de finales de los 70 el término "gótico" describía originalmente una «atmósfera opresiva», el término fue pronto aplicado a grupos específicos como Bauhaus, que continuaron la estela de Joy Division y Siouxsie And The Banshees. Generalmente, este tipo de bandas adoptaron «líneas de bajo potentes que tomaban un papel importante en la melodía y voces propias de la ópera, teutónicas y profundas al imitar a Jim Morrison o Ian Curtis».[cita requerida]

La evolución musical de Joy Division durante los pocos años que duró la banda, aunque paralela a la de otros grupos contemporáneos (The Fall, Magazine, etc.), es clave para entender lo que sucedería durante los años ochenta. Pasaron del punk al post-punk, y ya en Closer a un proto-tecno que podemos reconocer luego en bandas como Depeche Mode, Human League y otras. La segunda mitad de «Decades», el último tema de Closer, entierra definitivamente toda relación con el punk y anticipa el sonido de New Order.

Joy Division ha influido tanto a bandas coetáneas (U2 y The Cure), como a artistas actuales: Interpol, Bloc Party y Editors. Bono, cantante de U2, ha dejado claro que su grupo siente veneración por Joy Division. En su autobiografía de 2006, U2 by U2 cuenta que «sería difícil encontrar un lugar más oscuro en la música, que el de Joy Division. Su nombre, sus letras y su cantante fueron como la nube más negra que puedas encontrar en el cielo. Percibí esa búsqueda de un Dios, o luz, o una razón de ser. Notas que para él la belleza era verdad y la verdad, belleza y lo suyo era buscar ambas». Artistas como Moby, John Frusciante o You Love Her Coz She's Dead han declarado su estima por la música de Joy Division y la influencia que ha tenido en su trabajo. En 2005, Joy Division fueron incluidos junto con New Order en el UK Music Hall of Fame.

En 2018, se supo que el bajista original de Joy Division, Peter Hook, se había deshecho de todo su material que aún conservaba de la banda como consecuencia directa de su mala relación desde 2007 con el resto de los miembros originales (Stephen Morris y Bernard Sumner).[8]​ Hook decidió subastar gran parte de su antiguo material como guitarras, ropa y la entrada del concierto de los Sex Pistols, donde los cuatro miembros decidieron formar Joy Division.[8]​ Las razones por las cuales Hook decidió deshacerse de todo este material fueron, según el propio artista:

own_scenes.desc: De Warsaw, rock pesado con influencias punk, a la desolación ballardiana: la originalidad crece a medida que las canciones se vuelven lentas y ralas, con el bajo de Peter Hook llevando la melodía, la guitarra de Bernard Sumner abriendo huecos, la batería de Stephen Morris rodeando un cráter y Ian Curtis recitando desde «un lugar solitario». Martin Hannett, productor de Factory, convierte el espacio en «control atmosférico» con delays digitales y grabaciones separadas: Unknown Pleasures (1979), con la portada del púlsar de Peter Saville, «Transmission», «Atmosphere». El coqueteo con la imaginería nazi, la epilepsia, los barbitúricos y un matrimonio roto desembocan en Closer, «estar dentro de la cabeza de Curtis», y en su suicidio en mayo de 1980. «Love Will Tear Us Apart» es su primer hit. Los supervivientes empiezan de cero como New Order.

refs.q: Asimilando la desolada atmósfera ballardiana del Manchester de los setenta
refs.para: Asimilando la desolada atmósfera ballardiana del Manchester de los setenta, la música de Joy Division hace equilibrio en una delicada membrana entre lo local y lo universal, entre los datos concretos y específicos de un determinado tiempo-espacio histórico y lo atemporal de los miedos y los anhelos humanos. The Fall hiw algo bastante distinto: creó cierto tipo de surrealismo social, cierta visión narcotizada de la existencia proletaria manéhesteriana que sacaba a relucir lo absurdo, lo grotesco y lo sorprendente de sus corrientes subterráneas.

refs.q: Hannett usaba la AMS y otros efectos digitales que recién estaban saliendo al mercado
refs.para: "Digital", la primera colaboración de Hannett como productor de Joy Division, tomó su nombre de su juguete sónico favorito, el digital-delay de AMS. Hannett usaba la AMS y otros efectos digitales que recién estaban saliendo al mercado a finales de los setenta para conseguir "control atmosférico".

refs.q: Escuchar Closer es como estar dentro de la cabeza de Curtís
refs.para: Fieles a una represión emocional típicamente británica, ni sus compañeros de banda ni Hannett eran capaces de hablar honesta y abiertamente con Curtís acerca de sus problemas. Así y todo, sí parecen haber absorbido su dolor y haberlo recreado sonoramente. Escuchar Closer es como estar dentro de la cabeza de Curtís, sintiendo el terrible arrastre arremolinado de la depresión terminal. El lado A es pura agonía: el enjambre de afiladas navajas de ''.Atrocity Exhibition"; la mortaja de hielo de "Isolation", en la que Curtís suena como si estuviera envuelto en una neblina de barbitúricos, su voz mineralizada por los efectos de Hannett. El avance monótono de "Passover" se siente como si las baterías de la banda se estuvieran agotando. Lo sigue el rock duro, punitivo, de "Colon y" y de ''.A Means to an End", en la que la batería de Morris finalmente sí se desacelera y aminora la marcha, cual máquina moribunda.
refs.chapter: Cap. 7: Solo hazte a un lado: The Fall, Joy Division y la escena de Manchester

refs.q: El suicidio de Curtís a los veintitrés años lo transformó instantáneamente en mito
refs.para: El suicidio de Curtís a los veintitrés años lo transformó instantáneamente en mito. El mero compromiso del acto confirmaba la autenticidad de las letras y la música de Joy Division de una manera que era, a la vez, bastante problemática, perfectamente lógica y en última instancia inevitable. Como siempre lo había querido, Curtís se unió al panteón de aquellos que vivieron demasiado intensamente y sintieron demasiado profundamente como para poder existir por mucho tiempo en este mundo de medias tintas y conformismos. Quitándose las lágrimas de la cara, Factory se lanzó con entusiasmo a construir y alimentar la leyenda. Peter Saville le dio al single póstumo "Love Will Tear Us Apare" una exquisita tapa abstracta que se veía como el lustroso interior de mármol de un cenotafio. La tapa de Closer, de hecho, mostraba una fotografía que había sido tomada en un cementerio de Génova: un cuadro esculpido del Cristo muerto rodeado de abatidos dolientes.

scenes.name: Factory Records
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: El sello de Tony Wilson, presentador de televisión educado en Cambridge y admirador de los situacionistas. Peter Saville le da una identidad visual de austeridad modernista (Bauhaus, De Stijl, constructivismo); el catálogo numera cualquier cosa (FAC 8, un temporizador menstrual de Linder; FAC 99, la factura del dentista de Rob Gretton). Sin contratos, «continua negación a la ganancia» y una firme voluntad federalista frente a Londres.

scenes.name: Dark punk y rock gótico
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: El punk británico estuvo flanqueado desde el principio por un movimiento «gótico» que canalizaba su violencia hacia atmósferas de terror y rituales esotéricos: Stranglers, Siouxsie, X-Ray Spex. Lo más interesante evita el tono de película de terror: The Cure introducen la angustia existencial de Camus y Sartre (Pornography, Disintegration); Joy Division mezclan Doors, Kraftwerk y Black Sabbath y su final anuncia el synth-pop; Bauhaus, Killing Joke, Psychedelic Furs, los irlandeses Virgin Prunes y la cima del género, Public Image Ltd de Johnny Lydon, que convierte el punk en música de cámara con dub y ecos étnicos (Second Edition, Flowers Of Romance). Después, el gótico bailable de Sisters Of Mercy, Alien Sex Fiend, Cult, Mission e In The Nursery.

scenes.name: Post-punk / art-punk
scenes.book: Loops 1 y 2. Una historia de la música electrónica
scenes.author: Javier Blánquez (ed.)
scenes.desc: Tras el viaje de John Lydon a Jamaica nace el post-punk: PiL infecta de dub sus diatribas. El punk blanco se cruza con la música negra (A Certain Ratio, ESG, Liquid Liquid, Gang of Four, Shriekback, 23 Skidoo), Wire construye nuevos lenguajes, y Joy Division renace tras la muerte de Ian Curtis como New Order, que hermana post-punk y disco americana y prepara al Reino Unido para el house. Factory tuvo su propio club: The Haçienda.

podcast.title: Formation Inspiration (Spring 1976)
podcast.body: Bernie and Peter were motivated to form a band after witnessing a Sex Pistols gig in Manchester. Despite perceiving the performance as "terrible," they found it "great" in its spirit and decided that if the Sex Pistols could perform, they could too. Their initial group was called Warsaw, which subsequently evolved into Joy Division, and later New Order. "If they could do it, maybe we could."

"In the audience that night were future members of the buscocks and the pet shop boys and joy division and new order."

podcast.title: Discovery by Rob Gretton (1977)
podcast.body: Rob Gretton, a Manchester punk scene figure and DJ, discovered the band formerly known as Warsaw (now trading as Joy Division) performing at approximately two in the morning as part of a talent showcase in 1977. podcast.title: Early Sound and Aggression (1977-1978)
podcast.body: In their early years, Joy Division's live shows in 1977 and 1978 were characterized by an aggressive, punk-influenced sound. Ian Curtis displayed an aggressive stage presence, and the instrumentation often featured excessive reverberation, contributing to a somewhat "contaminated" sound, reflecting a preference for first takes. "Cuando vemos los conciertos que había dado Joy Division posiblemente en los primeros años, 77, 78, seguían siendo una banda bastante agresiva, vemos ahí en Cortis Cantardo, una muy agresiva, vemos esa reverberación excesiva a veces de los instrumentos, vemos esa contaminación que hace que no llegue a Sprite a la ende nada, en claro, es amor por las primeras tomas que los iba a grabar tan rápido."

podcast.title: Depression and Personal Turmoil (April 1980)
podcast.body: By April 1980, Ian Curtis was severely depressed, a state compounded not only by his epilepsy but also by a failing affair with a Belgian fan, the impending split from his wife, and dire financial difficulties that forced them to give away their family dog. He desired solitude but was ill-equipped to live alone. "By April 1980, Ian was very, very depressed. Not just as a result of the epilepsy either. He was having an affair with a Belgian fan. That wasn't going well. He and his wife were on the verge of splitting up. Money was so tight that they had to give away the family dog. He wanted to be alone but really wasn't equipped to live alone."

podcast.title: Final Concert and Seizure (May 2, 1980)
podcast.body: Joy Division's last concert was held at Birmingham University on May 2, 1980, and was recorded. During the performance of "Decades," Ian Curtis fainted on stage due to an epileptic seizure. The audience initially mistook his collapse for an intense dance move and cheered. Curtis was helped off stage, recovered, and returned for an encore, marking his final stage appearance. He died by suicide less than two weeks later. "The final joy division gig was held on May 2nd, 1980 at Birmingham University. The show was recorded."

podcast.title: Ian Curtis's Struggles (Spring 1980)

Despite the band's rising success and a booked American tour, Curtis was terribly depressed and considering quitting the band to open a bookshop on the continent. "Singer Ian Curtis was battling drugs in alcohol. He was having an affair with a Belgian woman while his wife went to work and cared for their baby daughter. podcast.title: Ian Curtis's Suicide (1980)
podcast.body: Singer Ian Curtis killed himself on May 18, 1980, at the age of 23. He had been suffering from severe depression, epilepsy, and substance abuse problems related to his illnesses, and had attempted suicide at least once before. His deteriorating condition was compounded by marital problems. The day before the band's first North American tour, Ian stayed up all night watching TV, listening to music, drinking whiskey and coffee, then hanged himself in his kitchen with a clothesline. His wife, Deborah, found him the next morning. "Ian had been suffering from severe depression, epilepsy, and all manner of substance abuse problems related to his illnesses."

podcast.title: 'Unknown Pleasures' Cover Art
podcast.body: The striking black cover design for "Unknown Pleasures" by Factory Records in-house art director Peter Saville featured minimal text and an image that appeared to be a mountain range but was actually a graphical representation (ridge line plot) of 100 consecutive pulses from CP1919, the first pulsar ever discovered, found in the Cambridge Encyclopedia of Astronomy. Saville reversed the original black-on-white diagram to white-on-black, creating an iconic image that launched countless t-shirts and a 2003 clothing line. "It was originally black on white, but Savile reversed it to be white on black. But what is this? podcast.body: In his final days, Ian Curtis, isolated and mentally/physically unwell, watched the Werner Herzog film "Strozek," about a struggling musician, drank strong coffee and whiskey, and wrote a long note to his estranged wife Deborah, with pictures of his wife and baby daughter nearby. On Sunday, May 18, 1980, at approximately 11 AM, Deborah returned home and found Ian had hung himself in the kitchen using an old-fashioned clothes rack. "Once Deborah was gone, Ian sat down to watch a movie on the telly. A 1977 Werner Herzog film entitled Strozek." "And within seconds, she ran into the street, screaming. Ian had hung himself in the kitchen using an old-fashioned clothes rack that could be raised and lowered from the ceiling using a rope and pulley."

podcast.title: Ian Curtis's Personal Turmoil
podcast.body: The lyrics for "Love Will Tear Us Apart" were deeply personal, drawn from the considerable turmoil in Ian Curtis's life. This included his epilepsy, which was growing worse due to drugs, alcohol, late nights, smoking bad food, and the stress of holding down a day job while being in a struggling band. His failing marriage to Deborah and an affair with a Belgian woman named Anaconda Rae also contributed significantly to his emotional state reflected in the song. "Curtis's lyrics were drawn from the turmoil in his life."

podcast.title: Internal Creative Discrepancies
podcast.body: Throughout the band's career, there were significant creative discrepancies, particularly between Martin Hannett's vision, supported by Ian Curtis, and the rest of the band, especially Peter Hook. podcast.title: Legacy and Influence
podcast.body: Joy Division was a foundational band for Factory Records. Following the suicide of singer Ian Curtis in 1980, the remaining members regrouped to form New Order. podcast.title: Limited Output Preserves Legacy
podcast.body: The fact that Joy Division released only two albums is highlighted as a significant factor in their enduring legend, as it "froze them in time," concentrating their entire output into a powerful, finite body of work that never had the chance to "grow stale and boring." podcast.title: Lyrics Reflecting Relationships
podcast.body: Specific lines in "Love Will Tear Us Apart," such as "why is the bedroom so cold and turned away on your side," are understood to be direct expressions from Ian Curtis, speaking to either his wife Deborah or his girlfriend Anaconda Rae, or both. podcast.title: Manchester's Influence
podcast.body: The band's rise in 1978 coincided with severe economic and social troubles in their hometown of Manchester, including closed mills, pollution, crime, high youth unemployment, and a crumbling sewer system during a hot summer, which created an audience for their bleak music. "Jordy Vision was also in the right place at the right time. Manchester, their hometown, was in big trouble. The mills had all shut down. What was left was polluted and full of crime. podcast.title: Martin Hannett as Novice Producer
podcast.body: Martin Hannett, a personal friend of the band, became Joy Division's producer. Despite his later importance in post-punk and UK music of the 80s and 90s, when he started with Joy Division, he was a novice who had never produced an album before. He learned production simultaneously as Joy Division learned to record and Tony Wilson learned to run Factory Records. "el primer LP que produjo Martin Jannett era el de yoidivisión y estaba aprendiendo a producir casi al mismo tiempo al que yoidivisión estaba aprendiendo a grabar y al mismo tiempo al que Toni Wilson estaba aprendiendo a tener una disco gráfica"

podcast.title: Martin Hannett's Influence on Sound
podcast.body: Hannett was crucial in defining Joy Division's experimental sound, emphasizing non-instrumental, background, and experimental textures. He was influenced by Krautrock, Can, and Cabaret Voltaire, and his obsession with sound purity led him to innovative recording techniques, such as individually recording drum components, which later became popular. "Martin Jannett si que es verdad que fue una persona muy importante para definir bien lo que sería el sonido de yoidivisión, fue los que más los ayudó a definir ese, toda esa influencia del sonido no instrumental, del sonido de fondo, sonido experimental, muy influenciados por el club rock, muy influenciados por can, muy influenciados por ese tipo de banda, es por cabaret bolter"

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Martin Hannett's Production Genius
podcast.body: For the "Unknown Pleasures" album, producer Martin Hannett (described as a "genius, but a certified wacko") radically cleaned up the band's sound and created its distinctive drum sound by rebuilding Stephen Morris's kit, reassembling it on the studio roof, and adding echo, reverb, and sound effects, isolating instruments to achieve an intimate yet cold, detached, and distant atmosphere, which became known as "cold intimacy." "Not only did he clean up the band's sound, but he's the guy who found that distinctive drum sound."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?

podcast.title: Martin Hannett's Production Obsession
podcast.body: During the recording sessions for "Love Will Tear Us Apart," producer Martin Hannett became intensely obsessed with the song. He meticulously recorded each instrument separately and spent a significant amount of time perfecting Ian Curtis's voice in the mix. His dedication was so extreme that he once called drummer Steven Morris at 4 AM, demanding he come to the studio immediately because he couldn't get the snare drum sound right, and frequently called the band in the middle of the night to hear the latest mix. "Hannet mixed and remix the song again and again and again."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Martin Hannett's Silence
podcast.body: Martin Hannett, their producer, rarely spoke about his life with Joy Division or his relationship with the band members in interviews. "Martin Jarek no nos ha dicho casi nada de lo que fue la vida de Joy Division o sueledad entre vistas y no le gusta hablar de esto."

podcast.title: Medication Side Effects and Personal Impact
podcast.body: The medication Ian Curtis was taking for his epilepsy caused wild mood swings. The fear of having a seizure while holding his baby daughter made him hesitant to embrace her, and he was known to suffer at least two severe seizures weekly. "The men, he was on, caused wild mood swings. When his wife gave birth to a baby daughter, Ian was afraid to hold her or less the seizure begin and he actually hurt her. He could be counted on to have at least two giant seizures a week."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Musicians Battling Disease Part 1

podcast.title: Military Vehicle Collector
podcast.body: Stephen Morris, the drummer for both Joy Division and New Order, is an enthusiast for military vehicles. His collection includes a Mark IV Ferret armored reconnaissance vehicle, and other vehicles that are described as "not quite tanks, but they're very close." He is known to drive these military vehicles on public roads in the English countryside. "I want to end with a story about Stephen Morris, the drummer for Joy Division and New Order. He loves cars."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Mini Riot at Derby Hall
podcast.body: On April 8, 1980, after Ian Curtis's overdose attempt, the band played at Derby Hall, where a shaky Ian was only able to sing two songs. The crowd reacted so negatively that a mini-riot ensued, resulting in five people being hospitalized. "Ian was so shaky that he was only able to sing two songs, and the crowd freaked out. Five people ended up being taken to the hospital after a mini riot."

srcs.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?

podcast.title: Missed American Tour and Triumph
podcast.body: Ian Curtis committed suicide just hours before Joy Division was scheduled to embark on their very first American tour. This tragic event occurred on the eve of what was perceived as a potential "gigantic, artistic, and commercial triumph" for the group. "Ian Curtis hung himself literally just hours before Joy Division was supposed to leave on their very first American tour."

srcs.episode: Death as a Career Move ｜ From the Archives

podcast.title: NME Cover and Fan Influence
podcast.body: Ian Curtis's appearance on the cover of NME in January 1979, wearing a dark raincoat, inspired die-hard fans to begin attending Joy Division gigs dressed in the same manner, highlighting the band's burgeoning visual impact and cult following. "When Ian appeared on the cover of the enemy in January 1979 wearing a dark raincoat, die-hard fans started attending gigs dressed the same way."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?

podcast.title: Name "Warsaw" Inspiration
podcast.body: After rejecting "Stiff Kittens," the band settled on "Warsaw," inspired by the song "Warzawe" from David Bowie's "Low" album, reflecting Ian Curtis's admiration for Bowie. "Besides, they were inspired by a song called Warzawe on David Bowie's low album."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?

podcast.title: Name Change from Warsaw
podcast.body: The band changed its name from "Warsaw" because it was frequently confused with a London metal band called Warsaw Pact. To avoid conflict, they just thought they would change their name. "Warsaw was always getting confused with a London metal band called Warsaw Pact. And rather than get into some kind of fight, they just thought they would change their name."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?

podcast.title: New Order Members' Reluctance to Discuss Joy Division
podcast.body: The members who went on to form New Order initially presented a united front to break from their past and focus on New Order, seldom wanting to discuss Joy Division in interviews. "El resto de miembros que fundaron New Order primero hicieron como un bloque frontal para intentar romper con su pasado y sentarse en New Order con igual nunca han querido hablar demasiado solo lo que fue Joy Division."

podcast.title: North American Tour Cancellation
podcast.body: The band was scheduled to depart for a North American tour on Monday, May 19, 1980, a tour that had every indication of making them famous. Ian's death the day before (May 18) meant the tour was canceled and the opportunity lost. "On Monday May 19, Joy Division was scheduled to leave for North American tour, and there was every indication that this was the tour that was going to make them famous."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?

podcast.title: Official End with Ian Curtis's Death and Closer's Release
podcast.body: The trajectory of Joy Division officially concluded with the death of Ian Curtis and the subsequent release of their album *Closer*. "con la muerte de Ian Cortes y la salida del club se muere oficialmente la trayectora de Joy Division."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Especial JOY DIVISION: 3. Closer y la muerte de Ian Curtis

podcast.title: On-Stage Seizures and Collapse
podcast.body: Ian Curtis's epilepsy frequently affected his live performances. During one studio session, he fell, hit his head on a sink, and lay unconscious. Strobe lights at a show once induced a seizure, requiring him to be carried off stage, an event that was not isolated, as he collapsed regularly during gigs. "One night in the studio, he fell and hit his head on the sink and laid unconscious on the floor. During a show that featured strobe lights, a seizure was induced and he had to be carried off stage. And that wasn't the first time. Ian collapsed during gigs almost regularly."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Musicians Battling Disease Part 1

podcast.title: Ongoing Legacy
podcast.body: Joy Division continues to generate a very important legacy today, both stylistically and, crucially, in the lyrical themes of Ian Curtis. "Han dejado muchísimo legado que sigue hoy en día."

podcast.title: Origin of "Joy Division" Name
podcast.body: The name "Joy Division" was chosen by Ian Curtis, inspired by a passage in Carol Satinsky's 1971 book "House of Dolls," which described "Joy Division" as a section in a concentration camp where women were forced to perform sexual favors for Nazi officers on leave, reflecting Ian's fascination with Nazi Germany. "The Joy Division was where women were forced to do sexual favors for Nazi officers on leave. I mean, how dark is that?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?

podcast.title: Other Health Issues
podcast.body: Besides epilepsy and profound depression, Ian Curtis also suffered from an allergy to sunlight, which caused his hands to become red and swollen. "He had many health problems. Depression was one. He developed an allergy to sunlight which caused his hands to go red and swell up."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Paris Concert (Pre-Ian Curtis Death)
podcast.body: A concert performed in Paris shortly before Ian Curtis's death was eventually released, although it suffered from terrible audio quality. "Hace pocos y se acaba de embinirlo un concierto que había nadado en París poco antes ya ha muerto de Ian Cortiso con una calidad de audio terrorífica."

podcast.title: Performance-Related Seizures
podcast.body: Ian Curtis experienced grand mal seizures during at least two performances, one triggered by strobe lights and another so violent that audience members feared for his life. His condition deteriorated to the point where even percussion effects could induce an epileptic episode, leading to a minder being assigned to ensure he took his medication, avoided alcohol, and got sufficient sleep. "There were at least two occasions when he had a grand mal seizure in the middle of a performance. One triggered by strobe lights and another that was so violent, people were genuinely afraid that he was going to die."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Last Moments Of - Part 1

podcast.title: Personal Turmoil and Suicide Attempt
podcast.body: Ian Curtis faced significant personal challenges, including a difficult relationship with his wife Deborah, who had initiated divorce proceedings, and an affair with a Belgian fan, Enneke van Array. On April 6, 1980, he made a suicide attempt by overdosing on pills, requiring an ambulance and a stomach pump, yet a doctor inexplicably deemed him not suicidal and sent him home, after which he was so shaky at a gig that he could only perform two songs. "There was a suicide attempt on Sunday, April 6, 1980 when Ian died a bunch of pills." "He told his mates that he had a terrible claustrophobic feeling like he was caught in a whirlpool of being sucked down and drowning."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Last Moments Of - Part 1

podcast.title: Peter Hook – Invented High-Register Bass Style Out of Necessity
podcast.body: Peter Hook developed his distinctive style of playing bass high up the neck — in registers typically occupied by lead guitar — out of the practical need to be heard in Joy Division's dense sound. This approach became a defining characteristic of post-punk and new wave bass playing and proved highly influential. "His unique style arose from the need to be heard, playing the bass in the highest notes of the neck."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt-Rocks Great Bass Players

podcast.title: Peter Hook's Bass Style
podcast.body: Peter Hook is recognized as a highly influential bassist, not necessarily for virtuosity, but for his distinct playing style. He treated the bass almost like a guitar, using it to mark time and provide a prominent melodic role rather than just a background rhythm. He often used a six-string bass, which was uncommon for bands of their genre. "Peter Huck tocaba el bajo casi como si fuera una guitarra, de manera que no uso el bajo o para hacer sonidos base, de fondo sino que marcaba mucho los tiempos, en muchas canciones de yoidivisión Peter Huck con el bajo es casi el que está marcando los tiempos."

podcast.title: Peter Hook's Shifting Perspective
podcast.body: Peter Hook has been the most vocal among the band members about Joy Division, though his perspective is possibly less objective due to his controversial relationship with Ian Curtis, and his narrative has changed significantly over time. "Tal vez el que más ha hablado ha sido Peter Huck y estrésse porque es posiblemente sea al menos objetivo porque tenga la relación como muy polémica con el propio Ian Curtis y su propio discurso ha cambiado mucho a lo largo de los años."

podcast.body: Joy Division was truly important during the 2000s Post-Punk revival, which saw the emergence of bands like Bloc Party, Editors, and Interpol, all showing their influence. "Luego en el 2000 tuvimos ese nuevo rival del Post Punk en el que salían, pues, blockparti en el que salían los editoros, en el que salían todas estas bandas de la nueva generación del rival del Post Punk, que era un fiel, y bien fue realmente importante."

podcast.body: The surviving members of Joy Division went on to achieve considerable success as the band New Order. "The survivors of Joy Division managed to do quite well as new order."

podcast.title: Post-Mortem Influence and Sales Surge
podcast.body: After the death of Ian Curtis, Joy Division's fortunes significantly improved. The band became recognized as one of the most influential post-punk bands of all time, and their records continue to sell in large quantities through multiple generations of music fans. The subsequent formation of New Order also contributed to increased sales of Joy Division's records by introducing the music to new audiences. "Joy Division's fortunes took off. They are considered to be one of the most influential post-punk bands of all time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Death as a Career Move ｜ From the Archives

podcast.title: Post-Mortem Legacy and Influence
podcast.body: Since Ian Curtis's death in May 1980, Joy Division has achieved legendary status, with continued album sales, radio play, streams, and hundreds of bootlegs in circulation. Their sound and style profoundly influenced the development of Goth, industrial music, Emo, and the alternative music scene of the 80s and 90s (through New Order), demonstrating how rock could be emotionally powerful, stripped down, intellectually serious, and a study in mental illness and emotional paralysis. "Since that day in May 1980, joy division has become legendary."

podcast.title: Post-Punk Era Pioneers
podcast.body: By early 1979, as the original punk rock scene declined, Joy Division found themselves perfectly positioned within the emerging post-punk era, where new sounds and attitudes constantly appeared, and their dark, moody, and depressing style resonated with a growing audience. "Joint division was perfectly positioned to take advantage of this. They found that there was an audience for their brand of dark moody depressing stuff."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?

podcast.title: Post-Suicide Media Attention and Increased Profile
podcast.body: Despite Joy Division not being widely popular in the UK, Ian Curtis's suicide, as a young artist gaining attention, became a major sensational event, gracing the covers of numerous music magazines and prominent newspapers like *The Sun*, which ironically gave the band a significant boost in public profile. "el suicidio de y ancurtis que son a grandísima convocción al final era una persona joven era una persona que estaba despegando estaba poco a poco captando atención y digamos que este tipo de tragedias y artistas jóvenes pues se prestando mucho a ciertos sensacionalismo entonces pronto lleno muchísimas portadas no solo de revista musical también de periódicos como de sangu y muchos periódicos importantes del reino nido se hicieron eco en partes importantes sobre el suicidio de y ancurtis y eso irónicamente le dio un punto bastante importante a la banda."

podcast.body: Ian Curtis's body was cremated after his funeral on May 23rd, and a headstone was placed in Macklesfield Cemetery bearing the inscription "Ian Curtis, 18580, Love Will Terrace Apart." This headstone was stolen in 2008 but was eventually replaced. "That headstone was stolen in 2008, but it was eventually replaced."

podcast.body: Prior to the release of "Love Will Tear Us Apart," Joy Division had achieved a certain level of critical acclaim but had not yet commercially "taken off." They faced challenges with record sales and public recognition, despite positive reviews, and considered "Love Will Tear Us Apart" to be an excellent and potentially breakthrough song. "nadie les compraba los discos, nadie se entraba de quienes eran y esta canción la consideraban buenísima."

podcast.title: Predecessor to New Order
podcast.body: Joy Division was the band that preceded New Order, sharing members before the death of singer Ian Curtis in May 1980. New Order initially retained Joy Division's dark, guitar-driven musical style. "Now, at first, New Order sounded a lot like Joy Division, which is to say they played dark guitar-driven stuff."

podcast.body: With the addition of producer Martin Hannett, described as a "crazy dude," Joy Division was able to carve out a unique niche within the post-punk scene with their dark, cold, and threatening sound. "And with the addition of producer Martin Hannet, who was a crazy dude all on his own, Jordy Vision created a niche all their own in the post punk world."

podcast.title: Professionalization and Career Focus
podcast.body: By early 1980, the band members had become fully professional, quitting their day jobs to devote themselves entirely to their musical careers. "ellos habían profesionalizado ya habían dejado sus trabajos para centrarse en su carrera musical."

podcast.title: Professionalization and Touring Issues
podcast.body: Following the success of *Unknown Pleasures*, Joy Division officially became professional, full-time musicians. This led to a complex and exhausting process of continuous touring. Initially, the band did not earn much money from concerts, forcing them to maintain a relentless touring schedule. This intense touring exacerbated internal problems, personal issues for Ian Curtis and other members, and financial difficulties. "con este disco yo oficialmente yo de visión ya se profesionalizan, ya pasan a ser una banda profesional, ya se dedican a esto a tiempo completo, empiezan ya un complejo y sobre todo hago tador proceso de gira continuada, que no consiguen ganar mucho dinero con los concertos todavía, entonces estaban como muy forzados, se están dando concertos de manera continuada, lo cual le irió sonaría bastante la banda, empezaron ya como a ver disputas bastante importantes entre los miembros."

podcast.title: Proposed Museum at Barton Street
podcast.body: There has been a persistent interest in transforming the house at 77 Barton Street in Macclesfield, where Ian Curtis lived and died, into a Joy Division museum, reflecting the ongoing fascination with the band and its frontman. "And the last I heard, some people still want to turn the house at 77 Barton Street in Mackelsfield into a Joy Division museum."

podcast.title: Punk Lyrical Innovation
podcast.body: With Ian Curtis as its lyricist, Joy Division inherited the punk rock tradition but propelled its lyrical content into an uncharted territory. They explored themes of psychology, intimacy, and personal suffering, which were largely unknown in punk rock at the time, offering a new level of depth and meaning to the genre. "Y en Cortis, que con Joy Division, hereda el PANC y lleva las letras, todo este rock PANC, una esfera prácticamente desconocida, en la que se habla, pues, de aspectos de psicología, de intimismo, de sufrimiento personal, que son increíbles."

podcast.title: Record Artwork and Cosmology
podcast.body: The song "Transmission" was chosen to start the show because it came from a record (implied to be *Unknown Pleasures*) whose artwork featured the radio telescope signature of a dying star, fitting a cosmology analogy presented at the beginning. podcast.body: There is considerable debate and controversy surrounding the precise timing and location of the recording sessions for "Love Will Tear Us Apart." This is largely attributed to the band's perception of the song as a career-defining piece, leading them to record it multiple times across various studios. "hay bastante controversias sobre cuando y donde se grabó el LoFwiki y la se apaga entre otras cosas porque como ellos ya la consideraba una pieza que iba a ser muy importante su carrera, la grabaron un millón de veces en un millón de sitios."

podcast.title: Reflecting Manchester's Mood
podcast.body: The "Unknown Pleasures" album perfectly captured the grim atmosphere of Manchester in the summer of 1979, a period marked by intense heat, a severe economic downturn, widespread unemployment, and the unpleasant odors stemming from the city's crumbling ancient sewer system. "Unknown pleasures captured the mood of Manchester that summer. It was very hot. The economy had gone very bad, and many people were out of work."

podcast.body: The remaining members of Joy Division, excluding Ian Curtis, were initially somewhat reluctant to experiment with synthesizers, keyboards, and more experimental sounds, a path they later embraced in New Order. podcast.body: Joy Division's performance on Tony Wilson's TV show "So It Goes" made a strong impression on Rob Gretton, who subsequently became the band's manager. "When they made it to TV, their performance impressed another guy, Rob Gretton, the person who would become Joy Division's manager."

podcast.title: Scrapped RCA Album Attempt
podcast.body: In early 1978, Joy Division attempted to record an album for RCA Records, but the project ultimately "didn't work out" and was completely scrapped before anything significant was accomplished. podcast.title: Screamo Band Preference
podcast.body: Screamo bands were noted for preferring "old Joy Division...records" over the music of bands like Weezer and Fugazi, indicating their darker, more intense aesthetic preferences and influences. "They preferred old Joy Division and Smith records over Weezer and Fugazi."

podcast.title: Second Generation Goth Influence
podcast.body: Joy Division records were a significant part of "second generation Goth" in the latter half of the 1980s, alongside bands like The Cure, The Sisters of Mercy, Siouxsie and the Banshees, and Bauhaus. "Along with the cure and the sister of mercy, choosing the banshees and some immortal Bauhaus and joy division records, there were a series of other bands that, well not exactly big in the mainstream, were huge parts of the cult of the Goth."

podcast.title: Self-Taught Musicianship and Technical Development
podcast.body: Unlike many technically mediocre punk bands, Joy Division's members, despite being self-taught (Ian Curtis, Peter Hook, Stephen Morris), dedicated significant effort to perfecting their technique and discovering new ways of playing their instruments. This commitment to unique approaches defined their distinctive sound. "yo división a un que era gente completamente autodidacta... perfeccionaron su técnica y hicieron mucho esfuerzo en perfeccionar su técnica y en descubrir maneras nuevas de tocar en contra de lo que estaban haciendo muchas bandas y es lo que acabó definiéndolo, lo apasionante del sonido de yoidivisión."

podcast.body: Under Rob Gretton's management, Joy Division signed with Factory Records, a "very cool, new indie label." Gretton's influence extended beyond Joy Division, as he also helped sign other bands, including Happy Mondays and OMD, to the label.

podcast.body: Lead singer Ian Curtis's jerky dancing style was attributed to his suffering from drug abuse and epilepsy, leading to paranoid and desperate lyrics that perfectly matched the band's minimalist music. podcast.body: Stephen Morris developed a highly personal, distinct, and experimental approach to drumming. podcast.title: Suicide Pact and Band Dissolution
podcast.body: A solemn suicide pact existed among the members of Joy Division, stipulating that if any member were to leave the band for any reason, Joy Division would cease to exist. Consequently, upon Ian Curtis's death, Peter Hook, Barney Sumner, and Stephen Morris honored their word, retiring Joy Division and beginning work on their next project, New Order. podcast.body: The other three members were devastated by Ian Curtis's death and had made a pact that if any member left for any reason, the band would automatically self-destruct. podcast.title: Uncategorizable Sound and Style
podcast.body: Joy Division, an archetypical British indie band from Manchester, developed a unique "strange spooky paranoid sound" in the late 70s. Their music was minimalist with Ian Curtis's distinct vocals, and live performances featured his "weird, strange, jerky" dance moves, influencing fans to adopt a dark 3-quarter length raincoat as an unofficial uniform. They defied easy categorization, being too dour for New Wave and not thrashing enough for punk, highlighting their distinctiveness within the post-punk movement. "By the late 70s, Joy Division had developed a strange spooky paranoid sound."

podcast.title: Unconventional Bass Technique Origin
podcast.body: Peter Hook, inspired by punk's DIY ethos, initially played bass without formal training. His bass was slung too low, his stance was wrong, and his amp was underpowered. To be heard over loud drums and guitars during pub rehearsals, he started playing parts much higher on the fretboard, which inadvertently advanced the sound of rock and roll. "So to cut through the din, he started playing his parts far, far higher on the fretboard than normal."

concerts.title: Birmingham University (May 2nd, 1980) – Final Gig
concerts.body: This recorded concert marked Joy Division's last performance. During the song "Decades," singer Ian Curtis fainted on stage due to an epileptic seizure, initially mistaken by the audience for an exaggerated part of his "unique herky jerky way of dancing." Despite recovering backstage and performing an encore, this was Ian's final appearance before his suicide less than two weeks later. "The final Joy Division gig was held on May 2nd, 1980 at Birmingham University."

concerts.title: Early 1980 Concerts - Shift in Sound
concerts.body: Concerts in the first half of 1980, including those in April and May just days before Ian Curtis's death, revealed a significant shift in the band's live performance, characterized by a reduced level of aggression, a much cleaner and more identifiable instrumental sound, and a clear movement towards new sonic territories. "en los conciertos de la primera mitad de los 80 esos conciertos que tenemos de abril y incluso de mayo de pocos días antes de amorte de Ian Cortes la banda ya había descendido bastante su nivel de agresividad en el concierto habían limpiado mucho el sonido de instrumentos el sonido era como mucho más identificable la banda se estaba moviendo ya mucha novos sonidos."

concerts.title: Final Concerts Pre-Ian Curtis's Death
concerts.body: Numerous Joy Division concerts from February to May 1980 were recorded, including one just 10 to 12 days before Ian Curtis's death, documenting the band's intense final period. "tenemos ya muchos conciertos bastantes están grabados de la etapa de febrero marzo abril e incluso mayo tenemos un concierto de 10 12 días antes de la muerte de Ian Cortes."

xref.title: Lesser Free Trade Hall Gig (1976)
xref.body: On Friday, June 4, 1976, just after 7:30 PM, the Sex Pistols played a pivotal gig at the Lesser Free Trade Hall in Manchester. Despite selling tickets for only 50 pence, fewer than 50 people attended, making it a "failed money losing gig." "Didn't seem like much of the time, but this failed money losing gig became a turning point for English rock."

xref.title: Death by Suicide (May 18, 1980)
xref.body: Ian Curtis died by suicide on May 18, 1980, at the age of 23. He had been in very poor health, suffering from epileptic seizures exacerbated by a "crazy cocktail" of prescriptions, drinking, illegal drug use, poor diet, and late nights. He also faced an impending divorce, an affair with a Belgian woman, money worries, and pressure to continue performing with Joy Division despite his problems. The final Joy Division show on May 2, 1980, saw Ian faint during the last song, experiencing another grand mal seizure, leading to the cancellation of their upcoming North American tour. On the evening of May 17, Ian returned to his home at 77 Barton Street in Macclesfield, Manchester. His wife Deborah was out. He watched the 1977 film "Strozek," drank strong coffee and whiskey, and then wrote a long note to Deborah all night. As the sun rose on May 18, he put on his favorite album, "The Idiot" by Iggy Pop, went to the garden for a length of rope from the clothesline, and hanged himself. Deborah found him a few hours later. "He'd been in very poor health, suffering from epileptic seizures that were exacerbated by a crazy cocktail of prescriptions, drinking illegal drug use, poor diet late nights, an impending divorce, and a ferry was having with a woman from Belgium worries about money and pressures to keep on performing with the band despite all these problems."

xref.title: Musical Evolution (1982)
xref.body: Initially, New Order sounded similar to Joy Division. However, a trip to New York, where they were exposed to post-disco, early house, and electro music, changed their direction. They became fascinated with synthesizers, drum machines, and sequencers, shifting by 1982 from Joy Division's guitar-based style to a more electronic and dance-oriented sound with Bernard Sumner fronting the band. "And by 1982, New Order had moved away from the guitar-based material that Joy Division had become famous for into something more electronic and dancing, all with Bernard out front."

xref.title: The Haçienda Nightclub (1982–1997) – Millions Lost, Band Driven to Near-Bankruptcy
xref.body: In 1982, New Order were convinced to invest in building and running a nightclub in their Manchester hometown called the Haçienda. Having no knowledge of club management, they poured millions of pounds into the venture across 15 years, nearly bankrupting themselves. All their New Order and Joy Division album revenues were effectively swallowed by it. The club was culturally important as ground zero for the rave and dance culture explosion of the late 1980s, but was plagued by financial losses, security problems, and drug-related deaths (patrons preferring ecstasy over alcohol made the bar nearly unviable). It closed permanently in June 1997 and was converted to condominiums. Bassist Peter Hook wrote a book about the experience called *How Not to Run a Club*. "The profits of which were largely lost in the sinkhole that was the Haçienda nightclub."

xref.body: Cornell died by hanging on May 18, 2017 — exactly 37 years to the day that Joy Division singer Ian Curtis hanged himself. xref.title: Early Awareness of Father's Music
xref.body: Natalie Curtis was 13 months old when her father, Ian Curtis, died. She first learned he was a singer when she was about three years old, told by her mother. As she grew up, she was mostly an "outside observer" to the Joy Division phenomenon but gradually became aware that her dad was the subject of much discussion. "She would have been 13 months old when dad died. What became of her? Well she first learned that dad was a singer when she was about three, mom told her."

xref.title: Evolution from Joy Division
xref.body: The band evolved from the dark, guitar-based Joy Division into a happier, danceier, synth and drum machine-driven group, showcasing a shift in musical style. "New Order had evolved from the dark guitar-based Joy Division into a happier, danceier, synth and drum machine-driven world."

xref.title: Evolution of Playing Style
xref.body: Over time, Flea abandoned his prominent slap-bass style in favor of a more melodic approach, characterized by fewer notes, more motion, and less frantic playing. This shift was influenced by bassists like Simon Gallup of The Cure and Peter Hook of Joy Division. "The slap-style has been all but abandoned in favor of a more melodic approach."

xref.title: Evolution to Electronic Sound
xref.body: Initially resembling Joy Division with dark, guitar-driven music, New Order quickly embraced synth pop sounds, drawing inspiration from Kraftwerk and other German bands. Over time, they incorporated more electronics, drum machines, synthesizers, and samplers, moving towards a more electronic sound. "But they very soon started bringing in synth pop sounds that owed more to a nod to craftwork and a few other German bands."

xref.title: Final Gig as Warsaw
xref.body: The band performed their last gig under the name Warsaw on New Year's Eve, 1977, before officially adopting "Joy Division." "So after one last gig as Warsaw on New Year's Eve 1977, Ian Curtis, Barney Albrecht, soon to become Bernie Sumner, Peter Hook and Steven Morris became Joy Division officially."

xref.title: Formation After Joy Division
xref.body: Following the death of Ian Curtis and the honoring of Joy Division's "suicide pact," Peter Hook, Barney Sumner, and Stephen Morris kept their word to dissolve Joy Division and immediately began working on their next project, which eventually became New Order. "So once Ian was gone, Peter Hook, Barney Sumner, and Stephen Morris kept their word. Joy Division was retired, and work was started on the next project, which would eventually be known as New Order."

xref.title: Formation and Early Amateurism
xref.body: Formed around 1979 just outside of London, at roughly the same time as Joy Division, The Cure initially consisted of amateur musicians, similar to many bands emerging from the punk scene. "The Cure from 1979, they were formed just outside of London at roughly the same time as Jordy Vision. And just like Jordy Vision, they were also pretty amateurish at playing their instruments, at least at first."

xref.title: Formation and Early Comparisons
xref.body: Interpol formed in New York in 1997 and, upon their emergence, were immediately likened to influential bands from two decades prior, such as Joy Division, Television, The Doors, and Lou Reed, establishing their sound within a specific lineage of alt rock. "They had come together in New York in 1997 and were immediately compared to bands we'd been around 20 years earlier, Joy Division, Television, even the Doors and Lou Reed."

xref.title: Formation and Influential Sound
xref.body: New Order formed from the surviving members of Joy Division following Ian Curtis's suicide in 1980. Their subsequent career proved as influential as their first, successfully bridging dance music with post-punk indie culture. Their Joy Division legacy provided unquestionable coolness and indie credentials. "When singer Ian Curtis committed suicide in 1980, the rest of the band regrouped as new order. That second act in their career turned out to be just as influential as their first."

xref.title: Formation and Name Origin
xref.body: After Ian Curtis's death, surviving Joy Division members Bernard Sumner, Peter Hook, and Stephen Morris discussed their future. Encouraged by their progress as Joy Division, they decided to move forward under a new name. Their manager, Rob Gretton, suggested "New Order" after finding the phrase in a newspaper headline about mass killings in Pol Pot's Cambodia. "Their manager, my name Rob Greten, is the one who came up with it. He found the name in a newspaper headline about the mass killings in Pol Potts, Cambodia. The phrase was new order."

xref.title: Formation from Joy Division
xref.body: Following the suicide of singer Ian Curtis in May 1980, Joy Division was reborn as New Order, with Rob Gretton continuing as their manager. xref.title: Increased Seizures and Mounting Pressures
xref.body: As Joy Division's popularity increased, the more gigs they played and the harder they worked, the worse and more frequent Ian's epileptic attacks became, suffering four grand mal seizures in one night in May 1979. By April 1980, the intense pressures from recording the "Closer" album, an ongoing tour, an impending North American tour, his failing marriage, guilt over fatherhood, his demanding mistress, and his continued use of alcohol and drugs exacerbated his epilepsy, making his mood swings unpredictable and leading to a state where he couldn't fall asleep until he had a seizure. "It got to the point where he couldn't fall asleep until he had a seizure."

xref.body: Following the suicide of singer Ian Curtis in May 1980, Joy Division was reborn as New Order, with Rob Gretton continuing as their manager. Gretton's involvement went beyond typical management, as he assisted the band with tasks like sorting song titles and even sang backup on some of their recordings.

"It worked quite well, especially with groups like Joy Division and Gang of Four and several others out of the UK."

xref.title: Second Generation Goth Influence
xref.body: Along with The Cure, The Sisters of Mercy, Siouxsie and the Banshees, and Joy Division, Bauhaus records were a significant part of "second generation Goth" in the latter half of the 1980s. "Along with the cure and the sister of mercy, choosing the banshees and some immortal Bauhaus and joy division records, there were a series of other bands that, well not exactly big in the mainstream, were huge parts of the cult of the Goth."

xref.title: Sex Pistols Manchester Show
xref.body: The Buzzcocks arranged for a still-unknown band, The Sex Pistols, to play the Lesser Free Trade Hall in Manchester on June 4th, 1976. This gig became mythical and legendary, inspiring about 40 attendees to form bands like Joy Division, Pet Shop Boys, Simply Red, and The Smiths, and to establish Factory Records. "They arranged for a still unknown band called The Sex Pistols to play the lesser free trade hall in Manchester on June 4th, 1976, a show that has gone down in myth and legend as one of the most important gigs in the history of rock."

xref.title: Vocal Coaching Influence
xref.body: During the recording of Joy Division's "Closer" album, Ian Curtis was made to listen extensively to Frank Sinatra records by producer Martin Hannett and Tony Wilson. This unusual coaching technique was aimed at helping Ian develop a deeper, richer, and more authoritative vocal delivery, which contributed to the album's haunting sound. "Why? Because they made him listen to a lot of Frank Sinatra records."
